questions: Where does the $100 injection enter the circular flow?
Who receives the injection as income, ready to spend it again?
segments.say: The circular flow: an injection enters. Government spending injects $100 into firms, and the money flows round the circular flow to households as income. Point at the injection arrow on your student notes diagram before any re-spending starts.

questions: How much leaks out in round 1, and as what?
How much is re-spent in round 2, and why not the full $100?
segments.say: Round 1: $100 in, $20 leaks out. Households spend the $100 with firms, but $20 leaks out as saving, tax and imports, so the token shrinks and only $80 goes round again. Now try the round questions on your worksheet.

questions: Why is each round four-fifths of the round before?
What is the running total after round 3?
segments.say: Rounds 2 and 3 shrink: $80, then $64. Each lap re-spends four-fifths of the last round, so the bars shrink geometrically while the running total climbs to $244. Check the shrinking bars against your student notes before moving on.

questions: Why does each AD shift get smaller?
How do you get the multiplier from $100 and $500?
segments.say: Aggregate demand settles at $500. On the AD diagram the same story shows as shrinking shifts: AD moves right by less each round until national income settles at $500, five times the injection. Keep the shrinking-rounds order as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
segments.watchFor: Every round re-spends the full injection, so national income grows by the same amount each round without limit. Listen for students who carry the full $100 into every round. Send them back to scene 2 and scene 3: Only part of each round's income is re-spent - the rest leaks away as saving, tax and imports - so each round adds a geometrically smaller amount and national income settles at a multiple of the injection.

title: The multiplier process: one injection, shrinking rounds
